Introduction: 绩效错觉转移的概念与背景

在管理学领域，"绩效错觉转移"（Illusory Attribution in Performance Evaluation）是指管理者在接受员工绩效表现时，由于受到多种认知偏差和随机误差的影响，将某些非能力性的因素误认为是员工真实的工作能力或潜力。这种现象本质上是一种系统性的认知扭曲，它使得管理者无法准确地区分员工绩效差异中真正源于个人能力的部分和源于其他外部因素的部分。当管理者将这些非能力因素（如工作环境、机遇、临时状态等）错误地归因于员工个人能力时，就会产生绩效评价的偏差，这种偏差在管理实践中被称为"绩效错觉转移"。这种系统性误差不仅影响到个人的绩效评估结果，还可能波及到组织的资源分配、晋升决策、培训投入等多个方面，最终影响到组织的整体效能和人才发展。理解绩效错觉转移的成因和表现形式，是提升绩效管理科学性和公正性的关键前提。随着大数据和人工智能技术的发展，越来越多的研究开始关注如何通过技术手段和制度设计来减少这种认知偏差对管理决策的负面影响。 <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-7-sonnet-20250219">

系统性偏差：光环效应、刻板印象与严格性偏差

在绩效评估过程中，系统性偏差主要表现为评估者在评价员工表现时所持有的固有认知框架和思维定势，这些偏差具有规律性和可预测性，会持续影响评估结果。其中，光环效应（Halo Effect）是最常见的系统性偏差之一，它是指评估者对被评估者形成总体印象后，这种印象会像光环一样辐射到其他评价维度，导致评价结果出现偏差。例如，当管理者认为某位员工"表现优秀"时，即使该员工在某些具体工作指标上存在不足，管理者也可能给予较高的总体评价。 <ExternalSearchUsed>

与光环效应相对的是严格性偏差（Stricter Standards），当评估者对某些群体持有负面刻板印象时，会不自觉地采用更高的评价标准。这种偏差通常与刻板印象（Stereotype）密切相关，刻板印象是指人们对某个群体成员持有的固定化、笼统化的看法，这些先入为主的观念会影响管理者对员工真实表现的判断。例如，研究发现，与男性相比，同样表现优秀的女性求职者更容易被贴上"不够有能力"的标签，这种性别刻板印象会导致系统性评价偏差。

这些系统性偏差往往相互作用，共同影响绩效评估的客观性。光环效应可能导致管理者高估优秀员工的表现，而严格性偏差则可能低估某些群体员工的真实能力。这种系统性误差的累积效应可能会导致组织人才选拔和培养的失衡，错失优秀人才或给予平庸者不恰当的奖励。因此，识别和纠正这些系统性偏差是提升绩效评估准确性和公平性的关键所在。 <ExternalSearchUsed>

随机误差的影响与控制

在绩效评估过程中，除了系统性的认知偏差之外，随机误差也是影响评估准确性的关键因素。随机误差是指在评估过程中由于偶然因素导致的非系统性偏差，这些误差既可能高估员工的真实绩效，也可能低估员工的真实表现。与系统性偏差不同，随机误差没有固定的偏向性，它们呈现出无规律的波动特征，在多次评估中可能会相互抵消。然而，当评估周期过短或评估样本量不足时，这些随机误差就可能累积，导致评估结果偏离员工的真实绩效水平。

随机误差的来源十分多样，包括评估标准的不明确、评估工具的信度不足、评估环境的临时变化、员工当下的身心状态波动等。例如，如果绩效评估指标设计不够科学，存在表述模糊或操作性差的问题，就容易导致不同评估者对相同表现给出差异巨大的评价。同样，如果评估工具经过多次使用后出现测量疲劳，其信度指标下降，也会增加随机误差。

为了控制随机误差的影响，管理者可以采取多种措施。首先，建立科学的绩效评估体系，明确评估标准和操作流程，确保评估过程的规范性。其次，采用多维度的评估方法，将单一维度的评估扩展为360度反馈、结果指标与行为指标相结合的综合评估体系。再次，增加评估样本量，避免以短期表现作为唯一依据，而应关注员工的长期表现趋势。最后，定期对评估工具和评估流程进行校准和优化，确保评估系统的稳定性和可靠性。这些措施的实施能够有效降低随机误差对绩效评估结果的影响，提高评估的科学性和公正性。 <ExternalSearchUsed>

基于人口统计学特征的偏差

在绩效评估过程中，管理者往往无意识地受到员工人口统计学特征的影响，这些特征包括种族、性别、年龄、民族、宗教信仰等。这种基于群体特征的系统性偏差通常源于社会中存在的刻板印象和成见，当这些先入为主的观念进入绩效评估过程时，就会导致评价失真。例如，研究发现，同样表现的员工，如果其姓名暗示其可能属于少数族裔，很可能会获得较低的绩效评价。这种现象被称为"消极刻板印象威胁"，它会使管理者在无意识中降低对特定群体成员的评价。

性别偏差是人口统计学偏差中最常见的形式之一。在多数文化背景下，长期形成的性别角色刻板印象会影响管理者对员工表现的判断。例如，研究显示，当同样优秀的求职者简历上的姓名显示其为女性时，相较于同性别但姓名显示为男性的求职者，她更可能获得较低的评价。这种性别偏差不仅存在于招聘阶段，在日常绩效评估和晋升决策中同样存在。

年龄偏差也是绩效评估中的常见问题。年轻员工可能被贴上"经验不足"的标签，而年长员工则可能被贴上"创新意识不强""学习新技术能力差"等刻板印象。这些基于年龄的预设会影响管理者对员工实际工作表现的判断，导致评价结果偏离事实。 <ExternalSearchUsed>

这些基于人口统计学特征的偏差不仅影响个体的绩效评价结果，更可能在组织层面造成人才断层和创新能力下降。当管理者始终戴着"有色眼镜"看待不同群体的员工时，就会错失优秀人才，限制组织的人才多样性。为了解决这个问题，组织需要建立更公平的绩效评估体系，通过培训帮助管理者识别和克服这些无意识偏差，并建立匿名评估机制来减少人口统计学特征对绩效评估的影响。

错误归因：能力与运气的绩效评估偏差

在绩效评估过程中，错误归因（Attribution Bias）是指管理者在解释员工绩效差异时所表现出的系统性偏差。这种偏差主要体现在管理者对绩效优异或不佳的员工所做归因的差异上。当员工取得优秀业绩时，管理者倾向于将其归因于员工个人的稳定特质，如能力、努力和责任心等内在因素；而当员工表现不佳时，则更可能归咎于外在因素，如任务难度、运气或环境等变动因素。这种归因模式的不对称性被称为"基本归因偏差"（Fundamental Attribution Error），它使得管理者在解释员工绩效时更关注个人特质而忽视情境因素。

错误归因在绩效评估中的具体表现形式多种多样。其中，"自我服务偏差"（Self-serving Bias）尤为常见，即员工在解释自己绩效优异时强调内在能力，而在解释绩效不佳时则强调外在因素。这种偏差在管理者评估下属时也普遍存在，导致评价结果的不客观性。此外，"虚假一致性偏差"（False Consistency Bias）也是绩效评估中的常见问题，管理者倾向于认为员工过去表现好的因素在未来也会持续存在，忽视了绩效表现的动态变化特性。

这些错误归因模式会显著影响管理者的决策判断。当管理者倾向于将成功归因于能力时，可能会给予更多奖励和发展机会；而将失败归咎于外在因素时，则可能给予更多宽容和继续培养的机会。这种归因方式的不对称性可能导致资源分配的不公正，使得真正需要改进的员工得不到应有的关注，而表现优异但存在潜力问题的员工却获得过度奖励。为了解决这个问题，组织需要帮助管理者建立更科学的归因框架，使其能够更准确地区分员工绩效差异中真正属于个人能力的部分和受到外部因素影响的部分。

认知与情绪因素在绩效评估偏差中的作用

在绩效评估过程中，管理者并非完全理性的决策者，其判断往往会受到认知能力和情绪状态的显著影响。认知资源理论（Cognitive Resource Theory）认为，人类的注意力和信息处理能力是有限的，当管理者在绩效评估时处于认知过载状态，或者信息处理能力受到限制时，就更容易受到各种偏差因素的影响。在这种状态下，管理者更可能依赖直觉判断而非系统性分析，导致评估结果出现偏差。

情绪因素对绩效评估的影响同样显著。管理者当前的情绪状态，无论是积极还是消极，都可能影响其对员工绩效的判断。这种影响通常通过"情感转移"（Affective Transfer）发挥作用，即管理者将自己当前的情绪状态投射到对客观事物的评价中。当管理者处于良好情绪状态时，可能更容易给出积极的评价；而在压力、疲劳或消极情绪影响下，则更可能做出保守或消极的评估。这种情绪依赖性评估（Mood-dependent Evaluation）可能导致系统性的评价偏差。

这些认知与情绪因素通常与其他偏差相互作用，形成复杂的评估偏差网络。例如，当管理者处于认知过载状态时，更容易受到光环效应的影响；而情绪波动则可能放大或缩小这种光环效应的强度。同样，当管理者存在刻板印象时，认知和情绪因素会强化这种刻板印象对绩效评估的影响。这种多重因素的交互作用使得绩效评估偏差更加复杂化。

为了解决这些问题，组织可以通过专业培训来提升管理者的认知评估能力，帮助其建立更系统的评估框架。同时，设计更科学的评估体系，如多维度评估指标、标准化评估流程和360度反馈机制，可以在一定程度上减少管理者个人认知和情绪因素对评估结果的影响。这些措施能够为管理者提供更客观的评估依据，降低认知偏差和情绪因素对绩效评估的干扰作用。 <ExternalSearchUsed>

管理建议与改进措施

1. **建立科学的绩效评估体系**：设计包含多个评估维度的综合评估体系，避免过度依赖单一指标。采用客观数据与主观评价相结合的方式，确保评估标准的透明性和可操作性。 2. **实施360度评估反馈**：通过上级、同事、下属等多方面的评价，相互抵消个人主观偏差。这种多源评估方式能更全面地反映员工的真实表现。 3. **延长评估周期**：避免以短期绩效作为唯一评价依据，而应关注员工的长期表现趋势。通过季度、半年度和年度等不同周期的评估数据综合判断员工表现。 4. **加强评估者培训**：定期对管理者进行绩效评估方法培训，帮助其识别和克服认知偏差。培训内容应包括各种常见偏差类型及其对评估的影响。 5. **使用评估校准技术**：对评估者进行定期校准，确保其评估标准的一致性。通过评估会议讨论典型案例，统一不同评估者之间的标准差异。 6. **实施盲评制度**：在关键绩效评估环节中，暂时隐藏员工的个人信息（如姓名、部门等），减少人口统计学特征对评估的影响。 7. **量化评估指标**：将尽可能多的评估内容转化为可量化的指标，减少主观判断的比重。对于难以量化的部分，也应建立明确的操作定义和评估标准。 8. **建立评估反馈机制**：允许员工对评估结果提出异议，并建立正式的申诉渠道。这种双向反馈机制有助于发现评估过程中存在的系统性偏差。 9. **应用统计控制方法**：使用统计学方法（如方差分析、回归分析等）对评估数据进行处理，识别和剔除异常值，发现潜在的系统性偏差。 10. **引入外部评估**：在必要时聘请外部专业机构进行绩效评估，利用其专业性和独立性减少内部人员可能存在的认知偏差。 11. **技术辅助评估**：利用人工智能和大数据技术建立评估模型，通过算法消除人为偏差。这些系统可以根据历史数据和客观指标提供更中立的评估建议。 12. **明确评估使用规范**：规定绩效评估结果的使用范围和方式，避免评估结果被用于与评估目的无关的领域，这种"评估污染"会放大绩效评估偏差的影响。 13. **建立评估效果监测体系**：对绩效评估结果进行持续跟踪，观察其与实际工作表现、员工发展、团队绩效等指标的相关性，及时发现评估体系中的问题。 14. **实施差异化评估策略**：根据不同岗位、不同发展阶段的员工设计差异化的评估体系，避免"一刀切"式的评估方式，这种针对性评估更能反映员工的真实表现。

Introduction: 绩效错觉转移的概念与背景

在管理学领域，"绩效错觉转移"（Illusory Attribution in Performance Evaluation）是指管理者在接受员工绩效表现时，由于受到多种认知偏差和随机误差的影响，将某些非能力性的因素误认为是员工真实的工作能力或潜力。这种现象本质上是一种系统性的认知扭曲，它使得管理者无法准确地区分员工绩效差异中真正源于个人能力的部分和源于其他外部因素的部分。当管理者将这些非能力因素（如工作环境、机遇、临时状态等）错误地归因于员工个人能力时，就会产生绩效评价的偏差，这种偏差在管理实践中被称为"绩效错觉转移"。这种系统性误差不仅影响到个人的绩效评估结果，还可能波及到组织的资源分配、晋升决策、培训投入等多个方面，最终影响到组织的整体效能和人才发展。理解绩效错觉转移的成因和表现形式，是提升绩效管理科学性和公正性的关键前提。随着大数据和人工智能技术的发展，越来越多的研究开始关注如何通过技术手段和制度设计来减少这种认知偏差对管理决策的负面影响。 <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-7-sonnet-20250219">

系统性偏差：光环效应、刻板印象与严格性偏差

在绩效评估过程中，系统性偏差主要表现为评估者在评价员工表现时所持有的固有认知框架和思维定势，这些偏差具有规律性和可预测性，会持续影响评估结果。其中，光环效应（Halo Effect）是最常见的系统性偏差之一，它是指评估者对被评估者形成总体印象后，这种印象会像光环一样辐射到其他评价维度，导致评价结果出现偏差。例如，当管理者认为某位员工"表现优秀"时，即使该员工在某些具体工作指标上存在不足，管理者也可能给予较高的总体评价。 <ExternalSearchUsed>

与光环效应相对的是严格性偏差（Stricter Standards），当评估者对某些群体持有负面刻板印象时，会不自觉地采用更高的评价标准。这种偏差通常与刻板印象（Stereotype）密切相关，刻板印象是指人们对某个群体成员持有的固定化、笼统化的看法，这些先入为主的观念会影响管理者对员工真实表现的判断。例如，研究发现，与男性相比，同样表现优秀的女性求职者更容易被贴上"不够有能力"的标签，这种性别刻板印象会导致系统性评价偏差。

这些系统性偏差往往相互作用，共同影响绩效评估的客观性。光环效应可能导致管理者高估优秀员工的表现，而严格性偏差则可能低估某些群体员工的真实能力。这种系统性误差的累积效应可能会导致组织人才选拔和培养的失衡，错失优秀人才或给予平庸者不恰当的奖励。因此，识别和纠正这些系统性偏差是提升绩效评估准确性和公平性的关键所在。 <ExternalSearchUsed>

随机误差的影响与控制

在绩效评估过程中，除了系统性的认知偏差之外，随机误差也是影响评估准确性的关键因素。随机误差是指在评估过程中由于偶然因素导致的非系统性偏差，这些误差既可能高估员工的真实绩效，也可能低估员工的真实表现。与系统性偏差不同，随机误差没有固定的偏向性，它们呈现出无规律的波动特征，在多次评估中可能会相互抵消。然而，当评估周期过短或评估样本量不足时，这些随机误差就可能累积，导致评估结果偏离员工的真实绩效水平。

随机误差的来源十分多样，包括评估标准的不明确、评估工具的信度不足、评估环境的临时变化、员工当下的身心状态波动等。例如，如果绩效评估指标设计不够科学，存在表述模糊或操作性差的问题，就容易导致不同评估者对相同表现给出差异巨大的评价。同样，如果评估工具经过多次使用后出现测量疲劳，其信度指标下降，也会增加随机误差。

为了控制随机误差的影响，管理者可以采取多种措施。首先，建立科学的绩效评估体系，明确评估标准和操作流程，确保评估过程的规范性。其次，采用多维度的评估方法，将单一维度的评估扩展为360度反馈、结果指标与行为指标相结合的综合评估体系。再次，增加评估样本量，避免以短期表现作为唯一依据，而应关注员工的长期表现趋势。最后，定期对评估工具和评估流程进行校准和优化，确保评估系统的稳定性和可靠性。这些措施的实施能够有效降低随机误差对绩效评估结果的影响，提高评估的科学性和公正性。 <ExternalSearchUsed>

基于人口统计学特征的偏差

在绩效评估过程中，管理者往往无意识地受到员工人口统计学特征的影响，这些特征包括种族、性别、年龄、民族、宗教信仰等。这种基于群体特征的系统性偏差通常源于社会中存在的刻板印象和成见，当这些先入为主的观念进入绩效评估过程时，就会导致评价失真。例如，研究发现，同样表现的员工，如果其姓名暗示其可能属于少数族裔，很可能会获得较低的绩效评价。这种现象被称为"消极刻板印象威胁"，它会使管理者在无意识中降低对特定群体成员的评价。

性别偏差是人口统计学偏差中最常见的形式之一。在多数文化背景下，长期形成的性别角色刻板印象会影响管理者对员工表现的判断。例如，研究显示，当同样优秀的求职者简历上的姓名显示其为女性时，相较于同性别但姓名显示为男性的求职者，她更可能获得较低的评价。这种性别偏差不仅存在于招聘阶段，在日常绩效评估和晋升决策中同样存在。

年龄偏差也是绩效评估中的常见问题。年轻员工可能被贴上"经验不足"的标签，而年长员工则可能被贴上"创新意识不强""学习新技术能力差"等刻板印象。这些基于年龄的预设会影响管理者对员工实际工作表现的判断，导致评价结果偏离事实。 <ExternalSearchUsed>

这些基于人口统计学特征的偏差不仅影响个体的绩效评价结果，更可能在组织层面造成人才断层和创新能力下降。当管理者始终戴着"有色眼镜"看待不同群体的员工时，就会错失优秀人才，限制组织的人才多样性。为了解决这个问题，组织需要建立更公平的绩效评估体系，通过培训帮助管理者识别和克服这些无意识偏差，并建立匿名评估机制来减少人口统计学特征对绩效评估的影响。

错误归因：能力与运气的绩效评估偏差

在绩效评估过程中，错误归因（Attribution Bias）是指管理者在解释员工绩效差异时所表现出的系统性偏差。这种偏差主要体现在管理者对绩效优异或不佳的员工所做归因的差异上。当员工取得优秀业绩时，管理者倾向于将其归因于员工个人的稳定特质，如能力、努力和责任心等内在因素；而当员工表现不佳时，则更可能归咎于外在因素，如任务难度、运气或环境等变动因素。这种归因模式的不对称性被称为"基本归因偏差"（Fundamental Attribution Error），它使得管理者在解释员工绩效时更关注个人特质而忽视情境因素。

错误归因在绩效评估中的具体表现形式多种多样。其中，"自我服务偏差"（Self-serving Bias）尤为常见，即员工在解释自己绩效优异时强调内在能力，而在解释绩效不佳时则强调外在因素。这种偏差在管理者评估下属时也普遍存在，导致评价结果的不客观性。此外，"虚假一致性偏差"（False Consistency Bias）也是绩效评估中的常见问题，管理者倾向于认为员工过去表现好的因素在未来也会持续存在，忽视了绩效表现的动态变化特性。

这些错误归因模式会显著影响管理者的决策判断。当管理者倾向于将成功归因于能力时，可能会给予更多奖励和发展机会；而将失败归咎于外在因素时，则可能给予更多宽容和继续培养的机会。这种归因方式的不对称性可能导致资源分配的不公正，使得真正需要改进的员工得不到应有的关注，而表现优异但存在潜力问题的员工却获得过度奖励。为了解决这个问题，组织需要帮助管理者建立更科学的归因框架，使其能够更准确地区分员工绩效差异中真正属于个人能力的部分和受到外部因素影响的部分。

认知与情绪因素在绩效评估偏差中的作用

在绩效评估过程中，管理者并非完全理性的决策者，其判断往往会受到认知能力和情绪状态的显著影响。认知资源理论（Cognitive Resource Theory）认为，人类的注意力和信息处理能力是有限的，当管理者在绩效评估时处于认知过载状态，或者信息处理能力受到限制时，就更容易受到各种偏差因素的影响。在这种状态下，管理者更可能依赖直觉判断而非系统性分析，导致评估结果出现偏差。

情绪因素对绩效评估的影响同样显著。管理者当前的情绪状态，无论是积极还是消极，都可能影响其对员工绩效的判断。这种影响通常通过"情感转移"（Affective Transfer）发挥作用，即管理者将自己当前的情绪状态投射到对客观事物的评价中。当管理者处于良好情绪状态时，可能更容易给出积极的评价；而在压力、疲劳或消极情绪影响下，则更可能做出保守或消极的评估。这种情绪依赖性评估（Mood-dependent Evaluation）可能导致系统性的评价偏差。

这些认知与情绪因素通常与其他偏差相互作用，形成复杂的评估偏差网络。例如，当管理者处于认知过载状态时，更容易受到光环效应的影响；而情绪波动则可能放大或缩小这种光环效应的强度。同样，当管理者存在刻板印象时，认知和情绪因素会强化这种刻板印象对绩效评估的影响。这种多重因素的交互作用使得绩效评估偏差更加复杂化。

为了解决这些问题，组织可以通过专业培训来提升管理者的认知评估能力，帮助其建立更系统的评估框架。同时，设计更科学的评估体系，如多维度评估指标、标准化评估流程和360度反馈机制，可以在一定程度上减少管理者个人认知和情绪因素对评估结果的影响。这些措施能够为管理者提供更客观的评估依据，降低认知偏差和情绪因素对绩效评估的干扰作用。 <ExternalSearchUsed>

管理建议与改进措施

# How standardized performance metrics reduce halo and severity bias–induced performance illusions

## Why halo and severity biases create illusions
Halo (or horns) occurs when a global impression about a target (e.g., a teacher's overall performance, a student's perceived quality, or a salient attribute) transfers to ratings of unrelated dimensions, inflating or deflating covariance across ratings and producing uniformly "high" or "low" profiles rather than diagnostic, attribute-specific judgments<cite id="f3268883-0">Halo effects occur when a general impression about a person or performance transfers to ratings of unrelated attributes, inflating covariance across ratings and producing uniformly high or low profiles rather than diagnostic judgments.</cite><cite id="f3268883-3">Halo in performance evaluation leads raters to assign consistently high (halo) or low (horns) ratings across dimensions, showing "too high and too even" correlations among dimensions.</cite>. Severity/leniency bias is a related pattern where raters systematically rate all dimensions more harshly (severity) or more favorably (leniency), again flattening differentiation and creating illusions of uniform performance or judgment<cite id="37fc81ff-7">Severity/leniency bias refers to systematically low (severity) or high (leniency) ratings across dimensions, which can mask true performance differences.</cite>. These biases arise from limited information, abstract criteria, general impressions, salient attributes, and rater factors such as low motivation or insufficient training<cite id="f3268883-0">Halo illusions derive from limited information (undersampling), general impressions or salient features (engulfing), abstract categories (insufficient concreteness), and rater factors such as low motivation/knowledge.</cite>.

## How standardization combats these mechanisms
Standardized performance metrics operationalize abstract dimensions into task-specific criteria and levels, reducing reliance on global impressions by forcing raters to evaluate concrete, predefined indicators. This design choice directly targets the sources of halo by constraining ratings to explicit evidence and decreasing the influence of salient global attributes<cite id="f3268883-4">Rater-mediated performance assessment research identifies insufficient concreteness and global impressions as key halo sources, motivating the use of analytic rating scales to reduce halo.</cite>. Pairing analytic rubrics with anchor papers (representative examples at each level) further calibrates raters to the specific evidence required at each level, which is recommended precisely to avoid the halo effect that can arise with holistic rubrics<cite id="27a4ea8a-4">Using analytic rubrics with anchor papers at each performance level is recommended to avoid halo effects and enhance rater consistency.</cite>.

Beyond rubric content, standardization includes procedures that improve reliability and reduce severity/leniency. Rater training and calibration teach raters to apply criteria consistently, avoid relying on global impressions, and not let performance on one task bleed into others, thereby weakening halo transfer and flattening profiles<cite id="37fc81ff-1">Training aimed at relying on the rubric as the sole criteria and avoiding cross-task carryover is used to improve reliability and validity of performance assessment.</cite>. Many-facet Rasch modeling (MFRM) complements standardized scoring by statistically adjusting for rater severity/leniency and making examinee scores "free of rater severity," while still enabling detection of individual rater biases that can be addressed through training or exclusion<cite id="83f5ff24-4">Many-facet Rasch modeling can provide scores free of rater severity while identifying raters with extreme severity/leniency.</cite><cite id="83f5ff24-3">Rubric-based performance assessments still show individual-level rater severity/leniency, but the rubric increases consistency in translating criteria to scores.</cite>. Designing analytic rubrics with attention to the order of criteria also mitigates halo by reducing construct-irrelevant order effects that can otherwise induce flattened profiles; randomized or carefully ordered criteria has been associated with smaller group-level halo in operational scoring sessions<cite id="f3268883-9">Rating criteria order affects the validity of ratings and can mitigate halo by preserving invariance of rating criterion difficulty; manipulating order reduced group-level halo in analytic rubrics.</cite><cite id="27a4ea8a-9">Manipulation of rating criteria order in analytic rubrics affects the validity of ratings and can be used to mitigate halo in operational scoring.</cite>.

Finally, procedural standardization—such as anonymizing evaluations—helps curb severity/leniency by reducing identity-based cues that feed into global impressions, with empirical findings that anonymous formats reduce bias in peer assessment compared to face-to-face formats<cite id="f3268883-5">Anonymous peer assessment showed the least bias, whereas face-to-face and online formats exhibited severity/leniency, suggesting identity cues contribute to bias.</cite>.

## Evidence that standardization reduces bias and illusions
Standardized analytic rubrics with concrete criteria and anchors reduce unduly flattened rating profiles and improve reliability, as shown in many-facet Rasch analyses where group-level halo is not detected under well-designed analytic scales and where separation indices and reliability indicate robust, criterion-specific differentiation<cite id="f3268883-7">Under analytic rubrics, group-level halo was not detected, and separation indices and reliability indicated reliable differentiation among criteria.</cite><cite id="f3268883-8">When criteria order was randomized, group-level halo decreased slightly, and reliability of separation increased, showing design features matter for mitigating halo.</cite>. Training and calibration procedures in performance assessment reliably improve inter-rater agreement, indicating that procedural standardization reduces inconsistent, bias-driven judgments<cite id="37fc81ff-1">Training and calibration were used to improve reliability and validity of performance assessment scores.</cite>. In educational measurement, pairing analytic rubrics with anchor papers is explicitly recommended to avoid halo and enhance rater consistency, reflecting a consensus that task-specific evidence reduces global impression transfer<cite id="27a4ea8a-4">Combining analytic rubrics with anchor papers is recommended to avoid halo and improve rater consistency.</cite>. In organizational and instructional contexts, standardization is also linked to more consistent ratings across dimensions, with rubric-based scoring showing higher correlations among evaluators and better alignment to overall grades than less standardized formats<cite id="27a4ea8a-6">Rubric-based scoring showed strong correlations between teacher ratings and overall grades and moderate-to-strong peer and self-correlations, indicating consistent rubric use across evaluators.</cite>.

## Limitations and best practices
Standardized metrics do not eliminate individual rater severity/leniency or all forms of halo; these biases may still be present at the individual level and require monitoring and mitigation<cite id="83f5ff24-3">Even with rubrics, individual raters can exhibit severity or leniency, though rubrics increase consistency.</cite>. Moreover, complex multi-criteria rubrics can sometimes induce criterion entanglement—where ratings on one dimension pull others—underscoring the need to design for clarity and to use anchors and training to maintain separability across criteria<cite id="f3268883-6">Rubrics can introduce attention bottlenecks and lead to criterion entanglement bias, where ratings across dimensions become similarly patterned.</cite>. Best practices include: using analytic rather than holistic rubrics, providing detailed anchors, training and calibrating raters to avoid cross-criterion bleed, sequencing criteria to minimize order-induced halo, and modeling scores with MFRM to detect and adjust for rater severity/leniency<cite id="27a4ea8a-4">Use analytic rubrics with anchor papers to avoid halo and improve consistency.</cite><cite id="f3268883-9">Manipulate rating criteria order to maintain invariance and mitigate halo.</cite><cite id="83f5ff24-4">Use many-facet Rasch modeling to adjust for rater severity/leniency and obtain scores free of rater effects.</cite>.

## Bottom line
Standardized performance metrics reduce performance illusions by operationalizing judgments into concrete, task-specific criteria and providing evidence anchors that constrain global impressions; coupled with rater training/calibration and careful rubric design, they lower the covariance and uniformity that halo and severity biases impose, yielding more diagnostic, reliable ratings across dimensions<cite id="f3268883-0">Halo stems from global impressions and abstract categories; making criteria concrete reduces reliance on such impressions.</cite><cite id="f3268883-4">Improved, analytic rating scales are a recommended strategy to reduce halo.</cite><cite id="f3268883-7">Well-designed analytic rubrics can eliminate detectable group-level halo and yield reliable differentiation across criteria.</cite><cite id="83f5ff24-4">MFRM can further adjust for rater severity/leniency, providing scores free of rater effects while enabling detection of remaining biases.</cite>.

Snippet: The research question posed in this study regarded the extent to which rating criteria order was associated with the magnitude of the group-and individual-level halo effects exhibited by 11 trained novice Korean raters. The results of a three-facet rating scale model suggested that no sizeable group-level halo effect across all three rating criteria orders was detected, as demonstrated in the acceptable fit statistics and halo indices in Table 11. However, the magnitude of the group-level halo effect varied depending on rating criteria order. For example, a similar magnitude of the group-level halo effect was detected in the standard-and reverse-order analytic rating rubrics, while a lesser degree of the group-level halo effect was detected when presenting the four rating criteria in random order. 

Although the difficulty measures of the four rating criteria remained invariant in both the standard-and reverse-order analytic rating rubrics, as indicated by 95% confidence intervals in Table 12, content and organization did not seem to maintain invariance in the random-order analytic rating rubric. More specifically, content on average received harsher or lower ratings from the trained novice Korean raters in the random-order analytic rating rubric compared to the reverse-order analytic rating rubric, while the difficulty measure of content remained invariant between the standard-and the random-order analytic rating rubrics. 

The rating criterion organization was more subject to rating criteria order than content in this study, as shown in its pronounced difficulty measure in the random-order analytic rating rubric in Table 12. The rating criterion organization on received much harsher or lower ratings from the raters when the raters used the random-order analytic rating rubric than when the standard-and reverse-order analytic rating rubrics were implemented. Snippet: The student evaluation of teaching have been proved to have many benefits, but it is acknowledged that the evaluation instruments used for assessing teachers by students often rely heavily on rating scales and rarely adopted open-ended items (Denson et al., 2010;Onwuegbuzie et al., 2009;Ren et al., 2023). This reliance highlights a significant debate in the field: how to balance quantitative assessment with qualitative feedback, and which approach better captures teaching effectiveness. As is well known, rating scales have lots of disadvantages: (1) Biased rating scores. It is recognized that rating scores obtained from Likert-format scales can be subject to biases ( Emerson & Records, 2007). Various biases can influence students' ratings, such as leniency or severity biases, central tendency bias, or contrast effects. These biases can impact the accuracy and reliability of the evaluation results, potentially leading to skewed or inaccurate understanding on teacher performance. Also, these biases challenge the validity of using standardized scales across diverse educational settings, suggesting that context-specific factors may not be adequately captured. (2) Variability in evaluation instruments. The instruments can vary significantly in terms of item quality, operationalization of the teaching-effectiveness construct, and specific dimensions included (Annan et al., 2013;Donnon et al., 2010). This variability can make it challenging to compare results across different instruments or institutions. Additionally, the development of evaluation instruments is often influenced by practical considerations, and psychometric evaluation of these instruments is not always systematically conducted. This can raise concerns about the validity and reliability of the evaluation process. (3) Haloe f f ect. The halo effect refers to the tendency for students to evaluate a teacher's overall performance based on their general impression or a single positive/negative aspect. This can lead to inflated or deflated ratings, where students' perceptions of one dimension heavily influence their ratings across other dimensions (Clayson & Haley, 2011). The halo effect can distort the accuracy of the evaluation results, as it does not provide a comprehensive and nuanced assessment of teaching effectiveness (Beran et al, 2007).

Title: Halo effects in grading: an experimental approach
Snippet: In the present investigation, participants rated two vignettes describing the academic behaviour and achievement of a student in two separate subjects. In line with prior research, we expected to find a halo effect in the grading of the second vignette. Participants who received the strong performance vignette were expected to rate the second average performance version higher than would the participants who received the average performance vignette or the weak performance vignette for the first subject and vice versa. 

As noted earlier, the participants of the study were students becoming teachers and teachers who were already working in school. As earlier research has shown, the assessors' judgments were affected by the expertise in the domain they were asked to evaluate. Thus, we controlled for the status of the participants, namely novices (meaning student teachers with less experience) and experts-in our case, practicing teachers. 

To sum up, to investigate the halo error we applied an experimental approach that used relevant information (grading on the basis of realistic vignettes). In addition, the experimental approach we took may be considered rather conservative-or as a rather pure reflection of implicit covariance theories-due to the fact that those halo sources depending on more category-irrelevant biases (such as undersampling, insufficient concreteness, insufficient rater motivation and interpersonal affect) were less likely to be found. Our study thus went beyond previous research in regard to three important concerns. First, we circumvented some of the methodological issues of previous research as outlined above. Second, we used relevant information as intervention material, rather than simply relying on the influence that additional information such as the attractiveness of the ratee, or single item interventions such as a rating of intelligence, can have. Finally, the experimental approach enabled us to reduce the influence of additional influencing factors such as stereotypes or affect, which are difficult to control for in non-experimental settings.

Snippet: Abstract Halo effects in teacher judgments, can occur when the assessment of one aspect of a person’s achievement is generalised to another aspect of achievement for that same person. We conducted an experimental study in which participants (N = 107) had to grade vignettes of the same student in two different subjects. The first vignette described either a weak, average, or strong performance, whereas the second vignette always described an average performance. Snippet: The term halo effect was coined by Thorndike (1920) in his work on employee performance appraisals and on ratings of army officers; since then it has been extensively researched (Forgas, 2011). It is claimed to be a pervasive cognitive bias in the assessment of achievement or performance (Cooper, 1981), and its properties have been discussed in depth (e.g. Balzer & Sulsky, 1992;Fisicaro & Lance, 1990). Dennis (2007) defined the halo effect (or halo error) as a 'bias [that] operates to inflate the covariance of different assessments by the same rater relative to those that would have occurred if the bias were absent ' (p. 1169). The achievement domain in which the effect is evoked can be similar to or essentially independent of the domain in which the initial assessment is made. Thus, halo errors are of potential significance in any setting in which ratings are used to provide feedback on performance (Dennis, 2007). This highlights their potential relevance in the school context in particular. 

Five sources of illusionary halo effects Cooper (1981) derived five related sources of illusionary halo effects that in practice occur together, namely undersampling, engulfing, insufficient concreteness, insufficient rater motivation and knowledge, and cognitive distortions. Undersampling refers to the rater's overestimation of the relation between two categories that results from insufficient information, forcing the rater to rely on a global impression. Haloed ratings from engulfing stem from the belief that either a general impression or, alternatively, a salient feature or features, is related to the categories being rated. In other words, these ratings are influenced by implicit covariance theories that link general impressions with the rated categories; such ratings are essential for the present investigation. Insufficient concreteness occurs when the nature of the rated categories is too abstract for the rater. Therefore, the rater is forced to merge their observations on the basis of the overlapping aspects of the presented categories. Insufficient rater motivation and knowledge can evoke halo effects if the raters expend insufficient effort on the rating process, or are insufficiently sensitive to the fact that their ratings might be influenced by a halo effect.
</snippet>

Snippet: The aim and objective of this article is to explore the issues and challenges of performance appraisals from the views and perceptions of teachers in selected Malaysian primary schools based on The Unified Evaluation for Education Services Officer’s documents also known as Penilaian Bersepadu Pegawai Perkhidmatan Pendidikan (PBPPP). This article attempts to understand the issues of the implementation based on the teachers’ experiences on the evaluation conducted by educational leaders in their schools. Performance appraisal is always stigmatized with the element of bias, and it is crucial to have clear perspectives of the teachers’ true experiences on the positional of this claim. For the analysis, a single explanatory case study based on qualitative methodology was implemented by adapting deductive thematic analysis method. In order to collect transparent data, semi-structured interview questions were designed using the formal appraisal evaluation form as reference. The selection of informants was using purposive sampling which involved five teachers with working experience between five to 30 years. The analysed data from the interview transcriptions and formal documents were divided into three themes: practice, implementations, leaders’ capabilities, and teachers’ experiences. Through the data, it is interesting to find that the contrast between the documents implementation and the actual practice carries out in schools. Snippet: In implementing performance appraisal, raters tend to make errors. There is a tendency for raters to be lenient or strict when giving ratings to ratees. In the former case, the rater overstates the performance of a ratee, that is, a ratee is rated higher than his/her actual performance. In the latter situation, the performance of a ratee is understated. A rate is given lower ratings than what he/she really deserves (Simmons, 2002). A recency error occurs when performance appraisal is based on the employee's recent behaviour, good or bad. The resulting performance review will be biased either favourably or unfavourably, depending on the way the performance information is selected, evaluated, and organised by the rater. Without work record or documentation for the entire appraisal period, the rater is forced to recall recent employee behaviour to establish the rating (Appelbaum, Roy & Gilliland, 2011). Cook and Crossman (2004) consider central tendency as a performance appraisal situation in which a rater tends to rate employees as average performers, thus becoming reluctant to give very good or very bad ratings. As such the ratings fail to discriminate either within or between people. 

Ratees' performance is considered to be the same irrespective of the different actual effort they exert. The halo effect is when a rater lets one particular aspect of an employee's performance influences the evaluation of other aspects of performance. Basically, a rater assigns ratings on the basis of a global impression of a ratee. In this case, a rater fails to distinguish among levels of performance on different performance dimensions. Conversely, a negative halo or devil's horns effect exists when the employee's ratings on all other dimensions is lowered inaccurately due to an accurate poor rating on one dimension (Grobler, Warnich, Carrel, Elbert & Hatfield, 2011).

Snippet: Performance appraisal refers to a systematic process of assessing the extent to which employees effectively and efficiently meet organizational goals and fulfill assigned responsibilities, based on predefined criteria [1]. Performance appraisals are closely associated with various job-related outcomes, including job satisfaction, individual performance, organizational commitment, job involvement, turnover intentions, and counterproductive work behaviors [2][3][4][5][6][7][8][9]. The effectiveness of performance appraisal systems depends on the degree to which both raters and ratees share a mutual understanding and agreement regarding the quality of the system. However, common sources of error in performance appraisal processes include deficiencies in measurement tools, biases associated with organizational policies, and rater-related factors-most often attributed to managerial judgment. In employee performance appraisals, raters may be influenced by various perceptual and cognitive biases, such as the halo effect, stereotyping, leniency or severity bias, central tendency, proximity bias, contrast effects, attribution errors, and other forms of rater bias, which can compromise the fairness and objectivity of the appraisal process [10,11]. When performance appraisals fail to accurately reflect employees' actual competencies and performance levels, they frequently result in dissatisfaction among both employees and managers, negatively influencing organizational efficiency and morale [12]. Park [13] highlighted that, to establish a more effective appraisal system, it was essential to consider the perspectives of employees and the motivational factors influencing managers/raters. 

Previous research has explored how rater motivation influences performance appraisal goals. Spence and Keeping [14] proposed four rating intentions: accuracy, conflict avoidance, benevolence, and impression management (i.e., controlling one's image). Khan et al. [15]. supported this framework by showing a significant relationship between rater motivation and appraisal effectiveness. Speer et al. [16] expanded this perspective by identifying five key motives: accuracy, coaching, encouragement, conflict avoidance, and system gaming, all of which shape rater behavior. Accuracy reflects the intent to rate employees in a way that objectively mirrors their performance.

Teachers need to retrieve reliable information on their students and apply this information in order to provide them with appropriate tasks (McElvany et al., 2009) and respond to their students' work with helpful feedback (Hattie & Timperley, 2007). As teachers often spend hours on end with their students, and thus have very extensive information on how each student is doing in class, it could be expected that their judgments would provide differential diagnostic information on their students' achievement (Spinath, 2005). 

Teachers' judgments are often the main source of information on the progress and achievement of their students. Thus, the need for valid assessment of students' academic achievement is of high significance. Research also shows however that the judgments were not perfect reflections of the students' abilities but may be influenced by a plethora of biases, such as stereotypes (e.g. Retelsdorf et al., 2015), expectations (Jussim & Harber, 2005;Muntoni & Retelsdorf, 2018), or halo effects (Dennis, 2007).

Title: The Effect of Rubric on Rater’s Severity and Bias in TVET Laboratory Practice Assessment: Analysis using Many-Facet Rasch Measurement
Snippet: Performance assessments such as laboratory practice in Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) are difficult to measure because they are subjective in their characteristics, which can cause bias. The use of a rubric scoring scale is suitable for measuring students' practical competency as it could translate the qualitative criteria into quantitative forms on a grading scale. The purpose of this study is to analyse the effect of rater severity for the performance of component installation of an electronic circuit project using Many-Facet Rasch Measurement (MFRM). Nine raters have examined the competency performance of 68 students using a four-point rating scale rubric consisting of 16 items. This study was conducted at three vocational colleges. Title: Effects of rating criteria order on the halo effect in L2 writing assessment: a many-facet Rasch measurement analysis
Snippet: The halo effect is defined as rater's cognitive bias, where the judgment of a certain rating criterion is influenced by that of related other rating criteria of test takers' performance. A body of research has examined the halo effect in the context of rater-mediated performance assessment (Andrich, Humphry, & Marais, 2012;Andrich & Kreiner, 2010;Bechger, Maris, & Hsiao, 2010;Engelhard, 1994;Lai, Wolfe, & Vickers, 2015;Marais & Andrich, 2011;Myford & Wolfe, 2003, 2004). More specifically, in operational scoring sessions, the halo effect induced by muted raters manifests itself as the unduly flattened profile of ratings, thereby significantly limiting the value of diagnostic feedback given to test takers and nullifying the additional efforts in developing multiple rating criteria. The sources of the halo effect have been known to entail rater's general impression, a salient rating criterion, and an inability of raters mainly induced by insufficient rater training (Lance, Lapointe, & Fisicaro, 1994). 

However, aside from these three sources of the halo effect, design features of analytic rating scales as the source of the halo effect have been relegated to a lesser position, although rating criteria order as an underlying mechanism of the halo effect has been suggested in rater-mediated performance assessment (Balzer & Sulsky, 1992;Fisicaro & Lance, 1990;Judd, Drake, Downing, & Krosnick, 1991;Murphy, Jako, & Anhalt, 1993). More specifically, the impact of design features on the halo effect was empirically demonstrated (Humphry & Heldsinger, 2014), and the results of eye-movement research on rater cognition showed that rating criteria order was associated with the rating process and rater severity in L2 writing assessment (Ballard, 2017;Winke & Lim, 2015). Regarding the effects of rating criteria order on the halo effect, Lai et al. (2015) clearly stated the need to control the sequence in which rating criteria are rated to identify which rating criteria are most vulnerable to the halo effect in L2 writing assessment.
</snippet>

Title: Halo effects in grading: an experimental approach
Snippet: Abstract Halo effects in teacher judgments, can occur when the assessment of one aspect of a person’s achievement is generalised to another aspect of achievement for that same person. We conducted an experimental study in which participants (N = 107) had to grade vignettes of the same student in two different subjects. The first vignette described either a weak, average, or strong performance, whereas the second vignette always described an average performance. Thereby, rich descriptions of achievement-relevant information were used, and the impact of influencing factors was reduced. The treatment condition emerged as a significant predictor of the grade given for the second vignette even after controlling for gender, status of the participants, and the gender of the student. The results suggest that participants’ ratings can be manipulated to show halo bias. The results support the view that teacher education should raise awareness of possible sources of the halo effect.

Title: Capturing fine-grained teacher performance from student evaluation of teaching via ChatGPT
Snippet: The student evaluation of teaching have been proved to have many benefits, but it is acknowledged that the evaluation instruments used for assessing teachers by students often rely heavily on rating scales and rarely adopted open-ended items (Denson et al., 2010;Onwuegbuzie et al., 2009;Ren et al., 2023). This reliance highlights a significant debate in the field: how to balance quantitative assessment with qualitative feedback, and which approach better captures teaching effectiveness. As is well known, rating scales have lots of disadvantages: (1) Biased rating scores. It is recognized that rating scores obtained from Likert-format scales can be subject to biases ( Emerson & Records, 2007). Various biases can influence students' ratings, such as leniency or severity biases, central tendency bias, or contrast effects. These biases can impact the accuracy and reliability of the evaluation results, potentially leading to skewed or inaccurate understanding on teacher performance. Also, these biases challenge the validity of using standardized scales across diverse educational settings, suggesting that context-specific factors may not be adequately captured. (2) Variability in evaluation instruments. The instruments can vary significantly in terms of item quality, operationalization of the teaching-effectiveness construct, and specific dimensions included (Annan et al., 2013;Donnon et al., 2010). This variability can make it challenging to compare results across different instruments or institutions. Additionally, the development of evaluation instruments is often influenced by practical considerations, and psychometric evaluation of these instruments is not always systematically conducted. This can raise concerns about the validity and reliability of the evaluation process. (3) Haloe f f ect. The halo effect refers to the tendency for students to evaluate a teacher's overall performance based on their general impression or a single positive/negative aspect. This can lead to inflated or deflated ratings, where students' perceptions of one dimension heavily influence their ratings across other dimensions (Clayson & Haley, 2011). The halo effect can distort the accuracy of the evaluation results, as it does not provide a comprehensive and nuanced assessment of teaching effectiveness (Beran et al, 2007).

If this was the case, as mentioned earlier, questionnaires could be much shorter, thus making students more willing to rate carefully and reduce block rating, as recommended by Feeley (2002). In any case, efforts to improve the psychometric quality of SETs to reduce the halo effect have been the concern of many researchers. For instance, Huybers (2014) proposed a best-worst scaling approach, which by construction forces respondents to consider the trade-offs between the items, thus enhancing discriminatory capability. 

However, not all authors accept that the halo effect is ubiquitous or even that it is necessarily problematic (Murphy, Jako, and Anhalt 1993). The latter point arises from halo effects being a problem of the rater, whereas evaluations, or performance appraisals in general, potentially remain informative, so long as they contain useable information on the average rating. Although the halo effect reduces the reliability of within-teacher distinctions by flattening the overall profile of ratings, on the other hand it can magnify differences in the mean ratings received by different teachers. It follows that the bias from a halo effect is not problematic if the purpose of SET is to distinguish a good teacher from a bad one, whilst it would be problematic if its purpose was to distinguish between strengths and weakness within a single teacher. In general, despite dissatisfaction with SETs, they remain widely used and are often the only instrument available to evaluate teaching quality.

In other words, rating criteria order as a common structural design feature could pose threats to the validity of ratings in rater-mediated L2 writing assessment. Specifically, with respect to the internal structure of the four rating criteria, it was empirically demonstrated that rating criteria order affected "the relationships among test items and test components" (AERA et al., 2014, p. 16) in that the invariance of rating criterion difficulty did not hold depending on rating criteria order, thus introducing either construct-irrelevant easiness or constructirrelevant difficulty (Messick, 1989). Consequently, it is plausible that the effect of rating criteria order upon the validity of ratings needs to be embraced by a framework of L2 writing assessment. 

The practical implication of the current research lies in the concrete recommendations of how to develop analytic rating scales to mitigate the halo effect among newly trained raters when assessing L2 writing ability. As has been suggested by Cooper (1981), the use of improved rating scales is regarded as one of the strategies for reducing the halo effect. In this respect, the results of the current study appear to provide empirical evidence for how to develop analytic rating scales.

# How standardized performance metrics reduce halo and severity bias–induced performance illusions

## Why halo and severity biases create illusions
Halo (or horns) occurs when a global impression about a target (e.g., a teacher's overall performance, a student's perceived quality, or a salient attribute) transfers to ratings of unrelated dimensions, inflating or deflating covariance across ratings and producing uniformly "high" or "low" profiles rather than diagnostic, attribute-specific judgments<cite id="f3268883-0">Halo effects occur when a general impression about a person or performance transfers to ratings of unrelated attributes, inflating covariance across ratings and producing uniformly high or low profiles rather than diagnostic judgments.</cite><cite id="f3268883-3">Halo in performance evaluation leads raters to assign consistently high (halo) or low (horns) ratings across dimensions, showing "too high and too even" correlations among dimensions.</cite>. Severity/leniency bias is a related pattern where raters systematically rate all dimensions more harshly (severity) or more favorably (leniency), again flattening differentiation and creating illusions of uniform performance or judgment<cite id="37fc81ff-7">Severity/leniency bias refers to systematically low (severity) or high (leniency) ratings across dimensions, which can mask true performance differences.</cite>. These biases arise from limited information, abstract criteria, general impressions, salient attributes, and rater factors such as low motivation or insufficient training<cite id="f3268883-0">Halo illusions derive from limited information (undersampling), general impressions or salient features (engulfing), abstract categories (insufficient concreteness), and rater factors such as low motivation/knowledge.</cite>.

## How standardization combats these mechanisms
Standardized performance metrics operationalize abstract dimensions into task-specific criteria and levels, reducing reliance on global impressions by forcing raters to evaluate concrete, predefined indicators. This design choice directly targets the sources of halo by constraining ratings to explicit evidence and decreasing the influence of salient global attributes<cite id="f3268883-4">Rater-mediated performance assessment research identifies insufficient concreteness and global impressions as key halo sources, motivating the use of analytic rating scales to reduce halo.</cite>. Pairing analytic rubrics with anchor papers (representative examples at each level) further calibrates raters to the specific evidence required at each level, which is recommended precisely to avoid the halo effect that can arise with holistic rubrics<cite id="27a4ea8a-4">Using analytic rubrics with anchor papers at each performance level is recommended to avoid halo effects and enhance rater consistency.</cite>.

Beyond rubric content, standardization includes procedures that improve reliability and reduce severity/leniency. Rater training and calibration teach raters to apply criteria consistently, avoid relying on global impressions, and not let performance on one task bleed into others, thereby weakening halo transfer and flattening profiles<cite id="37fc81ff-1">Training aimed at relying on the rubric as the sole criteria and avoiding cross-task carryover is used to improve reliability and validity of performance assessment.</cite>. Many-facet Rasch modeling (MFRM) complements standardized scoring by statistically adjusting for rater severity/leniency and making examinee scores "free of rater severity," while still enabling detection of individual rater biases that can be addressed through training or exclusion<cite id="83f5ff24-4">Many-facet Rasch modeling can provide scores free of rater severity while identifying raters with extreme severity/leniency.</cite><cite id="83f5ff24-3">Rubric-based performance assessments still show individual-level rater severity/leniency, but the rubric increases consistency in translating criteria to scores.</cite>. Designing analytic rubrics with attention to the order of criteria also mitigates halo by reducing construct-irrelevant order effects that can otherwise induce flattened profiles; randomized or carefully ordered criteria has been associated with smaller group-level halo in operational scoring sessions<cite id="f3268883-9">Rating criteria order affects the validity of ratings and can mitigate halo by preserving invariance of rating criterion difficulty; manipulating order reduced group-level halo in analytic rubrics.</cite><cite id="27a4ea8a-9">Manipulation of rating criteria order in analytic rubrics affects the validity of ratings and can be used to mitigate halo in operational scoring.</cite>.

Finally, procedural standardization—such as anonymizing evaluations—helps curb severity/leniency by reducing identity-based cues that feed into global impressions, with empirical findings that anonymous formats reduce bias in peer assessment compared to face-to-face formats<cite id="f3268883-5">Anonymous peer assessment showed the least bias, whereas face-to-face and online formats exhibited severity/leniency, suggesting identity cues contribute to bias.</cite>.

## Evidence that standardization reduces bias and illusions
Standardized analytic rubrics with concrete criteria and anchors reduce unduly flattened rating profiles and improve reliability, as shown in many-facet Rasch analyses where group-level halo is not detected under well-designed analytic scales and where separation indices and reliability indicate robust, criterion-specific differentiation<cite id="f3268883-7">Under analytic rubrics, group-level halo was not detected, and separation indices and reliability indicated reliable differentiation among criteria.</cite><cite id="f3268883-8">When criteria order was randomized, group-level halo decreased slightly, and reliability of separation increased, showing design features matter for mitigating halo.</cite>. Training and calibration procedures in performance assessment reliably improve inter-rater agreement, indicating that procedural standardization reduces inconsistent, bias-driven judgments<cite id="37fc81ff-1">Training and calibration were used to improve reliability and validity of performance assessment scores.</cite>. In educational measurement, pairing analytic rubrics with anchor papers is explicitly recommended to avoid halo and enhance rater consistency, reflecting a consensus that task-specific evidence reduces global impression transfer<cite id="27a4ea8a-4">Combining analytic rubrics with anchor papers is recommended to avoid halo and improve rater consistency.</cite>. The term halo effect was coined by Thorndike (1920) in his work on employee performance appraisals and on ratings of army officers; since then it has been extensively researched (Forgas, 2011). It is claimed to be a pervasive cognitive bias in the assessment of achievement or performance (Cooper, 1981), and its properties have been discussed in depth (e.g. Balzer & Sulsky, 1992;Fisicaro & Lance, 1990). Dennis (2007) defined the halo effect (or halo error) as a 'bias [that] operates to inflate the covariance of different assessments by the same rater relative to those that would have occurred if the bias were absent ' (p. 1169). The achievement domain in which the effect is evoked can be similar to or essentially independent of the domain in which the initial assessment is made. Thus, halo errors are of potential significance in any setting in which ratings are used to provide feedback on performance (Dennis, 2007). This highlights their potential relevance in the school context in particular. 

Five sources of illusionary halo effects Cooper (1981) derived five related sources of illusionary halo effects that in practice occur together, namely undersampling, engulfing, insufficient concreteness, insufficient rater motivation and knowledge, and cognitive distortions. Undersampling refers to the rater's overestimation of the relation between two categories that results from insufficient information, forcing the rater to rely on a global impression. Haloed ratings from engulfing stem from the belief that either a general impression or, alternatively, a salient feature or features, is related to the categories being rated. In other words, these ratings are influenced by implicit covariance theories that link general impressions with the rated categories; such ratings are essential for the present investigation. Insufficient concreteness occurs when the nature of the rated categories is too abstract for the rater. Therefore, the rater is forced to merge their observations on the basis of the overlapping aspects of the presented categories. Insufficient rater motivation and knowledge can evoke halo effects if the raters expend insufficient effort on the rating process, or are insufficiently sensitive to the fact that their ratings might be influenced by a halo effect.

Although LLMs offer potential advantages in consistency and processing capacity, it is crucial to examine whether they are susceptible to the same cognitive biases that affect human raters. Moreover, generational differences between newer and earlier models suggest potential differences in evaluation capabilities and bias susceptibility across different model generations, though systematic empirical examination is needed to understand these differences. 

Human raters are inherently susceptible to a variety of cognitive biases in performance evaluations, including but not limited to the halo effect, leniency or severity bias, and confirmation bias (Landy and Farr 1980 ). Among these, the halo effect stands out as a fundamental and pervasive bias in performance appraisals (Fisher and To 2012 ;Nisbett and Wilson 1977 ). For this study, we specifically focus on the halo effect due to its significant impact on performance evaluations. 

The halo effect occurs when an observer's overall impression of a person, object, or entity influences their evaluation of specific attributes, leading to unduly favorable or unfavorable assessments (Nisbett and Wilson 1977 ). This bias is prevalent in performance evaluations, where evaluators' general impressions of an employee can overshadow their objective assessment of specific performance dimensions (Balzer and Sulsky 1992 ). 

The halo effect is particularly significant due to its pervasive and unconscious nature (Nisbett and Wilson 1977 ). It can cause raters to overlook specific weaknesses or strengths, resulting in evaluations that reflect general impressions rather than detailed, attribute-specific assessments (Murphy et al. 1993 ;Thorndike 1920 ). This bias systematically distorts performance appraisals across various contexts, from employee evaluations to consumer choices (Asch 1946 ;Landy and Farr 1980 ). Its impact on decisionmaking can lead to unfair or inaccurate assessments (Fisicaro and Lance 1990 ), and it often resists correction even when raters are aware of its influence (Wetzel et al. 1981 ). These characteristics make the halo effect a crucial aspect to investigate in the context of LLM-generated evaluations, as understanding its potential presence in AI systems could provide valuable insights into the broader implications of cognitive biases in automated decision-making processes (Shrestha et al. 2019 ).

When raters fall prey to the halo effect, they transfer their assessment of a ratee's domain to another by providing consistently high (or low, or average) ratings across performance dimensions, even in the presence of disconfirming information (e.g., Borman, 1975;Nisbett & Wilson, 1977). Early work on halo showed that when superiors in the army had to provide a score for officers' performance on four different dimensions, they assigned ratings whose "correlations are too high and too even" (Thorndike, 1920, p. 27). Halo effects in performance evaluation has been shown in different professions: among public sector managers and non-managers (e.g., Belle et al., 2017), among post commanders and sergeants in a state police agency (e.g., King, Hunter, & Schmidt, 1980), among workers in a manufacturing company (e.g., Holzbach, 1978), and among students assessing faculty members (e.g., Jacobs & Kozlowski, 1985).

The halo effect is defined as rater's cognitive bias, where the judgment of a certain rating criterion is influenced by that of related other rating criteria of test takers' performance. A body of research has examined the halo effect in the context of rater-mediated performance assessment (Andrich, Humphry, & Marais, 2012;Andrich & Kreiner, 2010;Bechger, Maris, & Hsiao, 2010;Engelhard, 1994;Lai, Wolfe, & Vickers, 2015;Marais & Andrich, 2011;Myford & Wolfe, 2003, 2004). More specifically, in operational scoring sessions, the halo effect induced by muted raters manifests itself as the unduly flattened profile of ratings, thereby significantly limiting the value of diagnostic feedback given to test takers and nullifying the additional efforts in developing multiple rating criteria. The sources of the halo effect have been known to entail rater's general impression, a salient rating criterion, and an inability of raters mainly induced by insufficient rater training (Lance, Lapointe, & Fisicaro, 1994).

More specifically, the impact of design features on the halo effect was empirically demonstrated (Humphry & Heldsinger, 2014), and the results of eye-movement research on rater cognition showed that rating criteria order was associated with the rating process and rater severity in L2 writing assessment (Ballard, 2017;Winke & Lim, 2015). Regarding the effects of rating criteria order on the halo effect, Lai et al. (2015) clearly stated the need to control the sequence in which rating criteria are rated to identify which rating criteria are most vulnerable to the halo effect in L2 writing assessment.

Title: Capturing fine-grained teacher performance from student evaluation of teaching via ChatGPT
Snippet: The student evaluation of teaching have been proved to have many benefits, but it is acknowledged that the evaluation instruments used for assessing teachers by students often rely heavily on rating scales and rarely adopted open-ended items (Denson et al., 2010;Onwuegbuzie et al., 2009;Ren et al., 2023). This reliance highlights a significant debate in the field: how to balance quantitative assessment with qualitative feedback, and which approach better captures teaching effectiveness. As is well known, rating scales have lots of disadvantages: (1) Biased rating scores. It is recognized that rating scores obtained from Likert-format scales can be subject to biases ( Emerson & Records, 2007). Various biases can influence students' ratings, such as leniency or severity biases, central tendency bias, or contrast effects. These biases can impact the accuracy and reliability of the evaluation results, potentially leading to skewed or inaccurate understanding on teacher performance. Also, these biases challenge the validity of using standardized scales across diverse educational settings, suggesting that context-specific factors may not be adequately captured. (2) Variability in evaluation instruments. The instruments can vary significantly in terms of item quality, operationalization of the teaching-effectiveness construct, and specific dimensions included (Annan et al., 2013;Donnon et al., 2010). This variability can make it challenging to compare results across different instruments or institutions. Additionally, the development of evaluation instruments is often influenced by practical considerations, and psychometric evaluation of these instruments is not always systematically conducted. This can raise concerns about the validity and reliability of the evaluation process. (3) Haloe f f ect. The halo effect refers to the tendency for students to evaluate a teacher's overall performance based on their general impression or a single positive/negative aspect. This can lead to inflated or deflated ratings, where students' perceptions of one dimension heavily influence their ratings across other dimensions (Clayson & Haley, 2011). The halo effect can distort the accuracy of the evaluation results, as it does not provide a comprehensive and nuanced assessment of teaching effectiveness (Beran et al, 2007).

Title: Halo effects in grading: an experimental approach

As teachers often spend hours on end with their students, and thus have very extensive information on how each student is doing in class, it could be expected that their judgments would provide differential diagnostic information on their students' achievement (Spinath, 2005). 

Teachers' judgments are often the main source of information on the progress and achievement of their students. Thus, the need for valid assessment of students' academic achievement is of high significance. They have been studied extensively, with results showing a moderate to acceptable accuracy of teacher judgments for student achievement, their intelligence, or motivation (Hoge & Coladarci, 1989;Kaiser et al., 2013;Machts et al., 2016;S€ udkamp et al., 2012;Urhahne & Wijnia, 2021). snippet.text: The student evaluation of teaching have been proved to have many benefits, but it is acknowledged that the evaluation instruments used for assessing teachers by students often rely heavily on rating scales and rarely adopted open-ended items (Denson et al., 2010;Onwuegbuzie et al., 2009;Ren et al., 2023). As is well known, rating scales have lots of disadvantages: (1) Biased rating scores. It is recognized that rating scores obtained from Likert-format scales can be subject to biases ( Emerson & Records, 2007). Various biases can influence students' ratings, such as leniency or severity biases, central tendency bias, or contrast effects. These biases can impact the accuracy and reliability of the evaluation results, potentially leading to skewed or inaccurate understanding on teacher performance. Also, these biases challenge the validity of using standardized scales across diverse educational settings, suggesting that context-specific factors may not be adequately captured. (2) Variability in evaluation instruments. The instruments can vary significantly in terms of item quality, operationalization of the teaching-effectiveness construct, and specific dimensions included (Annan et al., 2013;Donnon et al., 2010). This variability can make it challenging to compare results across different instruments or institutions. Additionally, the development of evaluation instruments is often influenced by practical considerations, and psychometric evaluation of these instruments is not always systematically conducted. This can raise concerns about the validity and reliability of the evaluation process. (3) Haloe f f ect. The halo effect refers to the tendency for students to evaluate a teacher's overall performance based on their general impression or a single positive/negative aspect. This can lead to inflated or deflated ratings, where students' perceptions of one dimension heavily influence their ratings across other dimensions (Clayson & Haley, 2011). The halo effect can distort the accuracy of the evaluation results, as it does not provide a comprehensive and nuanced assessment of teaching effectiveness (Beran et al, 2007).

As teachers often spend hours on end with their students, and thus have very extensive information on how each student is doing in class, it could be expected that their judgments would provide differential diagnostic information on their students' achievement (Spinath, 2005). 

Teachers' judgments are often the main source of information on the progress and achievement of their students. Thus, the need for valid assessment of students' academic achievement is of high significance. They have been studied extensively, with results showing a moderate to acceptable accuracy of teacher judgments for student achievement, their intelligence, or motivation (Hoge & Coladarci, 1989;Kaiser et al., 2013;Machts et al., 2016;S€ udkamp et al., 2012;Urhahne & Wijnia, 2021). Research also shows however that the judgments were not perfect reflections of the students' abilities but may be influenced by a plethora of biases, such as stereotypes (e.g. Retelsdorf et al., 2015), expectations (Jussim & Harber, 2005;Muntoni & Retelsdorf, 2018), or halo effects (Dennis, 2007). 

In the present study, we focussed on a halo effect in teachers' judgement, which can occur when the assessment of one aspect of someone's achievement is transferred to another aspect of achievement in that same person. To that end, we conducted an experimental study in which teachers and student teachers had to grade vignettes of the same student in two different subjects. documents.snippet: The student evaluation of teaching have been proved to have many benefits, but it is acknowledged that the evaluation instruments used for assessing teachers by students often rely heavily on rating scales and rarely adopted open-ended items (Denson et al., 2010;Onwuegbuzie et al., 2009;Ren et al., 2023). This reliance highlights a significant debate in the field: how to balance quantitative assessment with qualitative feedback, and which approach better captures teaching effectiveness. As is well known, rating scales have lots of disadvantages: (1) Biased rating scores. It is recognized that rating scores obtained from Likert-format scales can be subject to biases ( Emerson & Records, 2007). Various biases can influence students' ratings, such as leniency or severity biases, central tendency bias, or contrast effects. These biases can impact the accuracy and reliability of the evaluation results, potentially leading to skewed or inaccurate understanding on teacher performance. Also, these biases challenge the validity of using standardized scales across diverse educational settings, suggesting that context-specific factors may not be adequately captured. (2) Variability in evaluation instruments. The instruments can vary significantly in terms of item quality, operationalization of the teaching-effectiveness construct, and specific dimensions included (Annan et al., 2013;Donnon et al., 2010). This variability can make it challenging to compare results across different instruments or institutions. Additionally, the development of evaluation instruments is often influenced by practical considerations, and psychometric evaluation of these instruments is not always systematically conducted. This can raise concerns about the validity and reliability of the evaluation process. (3) Haloe f f ect. The halo effect refers to the tendency for students to evaluate a teacher's overall performance based on their general impression or a single positive/negative aspect. This can lead to inflated or deflated ratings, where students' perceptions of one dimension heavily influence their ratings across other dimensions (Clayson & Haley, 2011). The halo effect can distort the accuracy of the evaluation results, as it does not provide a comprehensive and nuanced assessment of teaching effectiveness (Beran et al, 2007).

First, each rater rated the performances of five student-teachers separately. Then, their ratings were compared to identify points of disagreement. If the two raters' ratings differed substantially from those of the supervisor and they could not achieve consensus, the supervisor would function as a third rater to resolve the discrepancies. documents.title: Halo effects in grading: an experimental approach
documents.snippet:
In the present investigation, participants rated two vignettes describing the academic behaviour and achievement of a student in two separate subjects. In line with prior research, we expected to find a halo effect in the grading of the second vignette. Participants who received the strong performance vignette were expected to rate the second average performance version higher than would the participants who received the average performance vignette or the weak performance vignette for the first subject and vice versa. 

As noted earlier, the participants of the study were students becoming teachers and teachers who were already working in school. As earlier research has shown, the assessors' judgments were affected by the expertise in the domain they were asked to evaluate. Thus, we controlled for the status of the participants, namely novices (meaning student teachers with less experience) and experts-in our case, practicing teachers. 

To sum up, to investigate the halo error we applied an experimental approach that used relevant information (grading on the basis of realistic vignettes). In addition, the experimental approach we took may be considered rather conservative-or as a rather pure reflection of implicit covariance theories-due to the fact that those halo sources depending on more category-irrelevant biases (such as undersampling, insufficient concreteness, insufficient rater motivation and interpersonal affect) were less likely to be found. Our study thus went beyond previous research in regard to three important concerns. First, we circumvented some of the methodological issues of previous research as outlined above. Second, we used relevant information as intervention material, rather than simply relying on the influence that additional information such as the attractiveness of the ratee, or single item interventions such as a rating of intelligence, can have. Finally, the experimental approach enabled us to reduce the influence of additional influencing factors such as stereotypes or affect, which are difficult to control for in non-experimental settings.

documents.snippet: Abstract Halo effects in teacher judgments, can occur when the assessment of one aspect of a person’s achievement is generalised to another aspect of achievement for that same person. We conducted an experimental study in which participants (N = 107) had to grade vignettes of the same student in two different subjects. The first vignette described either a weak, average, or strong performance, whereas the second vignette always described an average performance. Thereby, rich descriptions of achievement-relevant information were used, and the impact of influencing factors was reduced. The treatment condition emerged as a significant predictor of the grade given for the second vignette even after controlling for gender, status of the participants, and the gender of the student. The results suggest that participants’ ratings can be manipulated to show halo bias. The results support the view that teacher education should raise awareness of possible sources of the halo effect.

The term halo effect was coined by Thorndike (1920) in his work on employee performance appraisals and on ratings of army officers; since then it has been extensively researched (Forgas, 2011). It is claimed to be a pervasive cognitive bias in the assessment of achievement or performance (Cooper, 1981), and its properties have been discussed in depth (e.g. Balzer & Sulsky, 1992;Fisicaro & Lance, 1990). Dennis (2007) defined the halo effect (or halo error) as a 'bias [that] operates to inflate the covariance of different assessments by the same rater relative to those that would have occurred if the bias were absent ' (p. 1169). The achievement domain in which the effect is evoked can be similar to or essentially independent of the domain in which the initial assessment is made. Thus, halo errors are of potential significance in any setting in which ratings are used to provide feedback on performance (Dennis, 2007). This highlights their potential relevance in the school context in particular. 

Five sources of illusionary halo effects Cooper (1981) derived five related sources of illusionary halo effects that in practice occur together, namely undersampling, engulfing, insufficient concreteness, insufficient rater motivation and knowledge, and cognitive distortions. Undersampling refers to the rater's overestimation of the relation between two categories that results from insufficient information, forcing the rater to rely on a global impression. Haloed ratings from engulfing stem from the belief that either a general impression or, alternatively, a salient feature or features, is related to the categories being rated. In other words, these ratings are influenced by implicit covariance theories that link general impressions with the rated categories; such ratings are essential for the present investigation. Insufficient concreteness occurs when the nature of the rated categories is too abstract for the rater. Therefore, the rater is forced to merge their observations on the basis of the overlapping aspects of the presented categories. Insufficient rater motivation and knowledge can evoke halo effects if the raters expend insufficient effort on the rating process, or are insufficiently sensitive to the fact that their ratings might be influenced by a halo effect.

The documents are used as formal documents in teachers’ performance appraisal evaluation since 2016. This article attempts to understand the issues of the implementation based on the teachers’ experiences on the evaluation conducted by educational leaders in their schools. Performance appraisal is always stigmatized with the element of bias, and it is crucial to have clear perspectives of the teachers’ true experiences on the positional of this claim. For the analysis, a single explanatory case study based on qualitative methodology was implemented by adapting deductive thematic analysis method. In order to collect transparent data, semi-structured interview questions were designed using the formal appraisal evaluation form as reference. The selection of informants was using purposive sampling which involved five teachers with working experience between five to 30 years. The analysed data from the interview transcriptions and formal documents were divided into three themes: practice, implementations, leaders’ capabilities, and teachers’ experiences. Through the data, it is interesting to find that the contrast between the documents implementation and the actual practice carries out in schools. Halo effect is one of the leadership biases which frequently occurred based on the data collected. This study could be a reference to the school and educational leaders to thoroughly examine the reality and capabilities of the school leaders to reduce bias in education service officers’ performance appraisal.

In implementing performance appraisal, raters tend to make errors. There is a tendency for raters to be lenient or strict when giving ratings to ratees. In the former case, the rater overstates the performance of a ratee, that is, a ratee is rated higher than his/her actual performance. In the latter situation, the performance of a ratee is understated. A rate is given lower ratings than what he/she really deserves (Simmons, 2002). A recency error occurs when performance appraisal is based on the employee's recent behaviour, good or bad. The resulting performance review will be biased either favourably or unfavourably, depending on the way the performance information is selected, evaluated, and organised by the rater. Without work record or documentation for the entire appraisal period, the rater is forced to recall recent employee behaviour to establish the rating (Appelbaum, Roy & Gilliland, 2011). Cook and Crossman (2004) consider central tendency as a performance appraisal situation in which a rater tends to rate employees as average performers, thus becoming reluctant to give very good or very bad ratings. As such the ratings fail to discriminate either within or between people. 

Ratees' performance is considered to be the same irrespective of the different actual effort they exert. The halo effect is when a rater lets one particular aspect of an employee's performance influences the evaluation of other aspects of performance. Basically, a rater assigns ratings on the basis of a global impression of a ratee. In this case, a rater fails to distinguish among levels of performance on different performance dimensions. Conversely, a negative halo or devil's horns effect exists when the employee's ratings on all other dimensions is lowered inaccurately due to an accurate poor rating on one dimension (Grobler, Warnich, Carrel, Elbert & Hatfield, 2011).

Performance appraisal refers to a systematic process of assessing the extent to which employees effectively and efficiently meet organizational goals and fulfill assigned responsibilities, based on predefined criteria [1]. Performance appraisals are closely associated with various job-related outcomes, including job satisfaction, individual performance, organizational commitment, job involvement, turnover intentions, and counterproductive work behaviors [2][3][4][5][6][7][8][9]. The effectiveness of performance appraisal systems depends on the degree to which both raters and ratees share a mutual understanding and agreement regarding the quality of the system. However, common sources of error in performance appraisal processes include deficiencies in measurement tools, biases associated with organizational policies, and rater-related factors-most often attributed to managerial judgment. In employee performance appraisals, raters may be influenced by various perceptual and cognitive biases, such as the halo effect, stereotyping, leniency or severity bias, central tendency, proximity bias, contrast effects, attribution errors, and other forms of rater bias, which can compromise the fairness and objectivity of the appraisal process [10,11]. When performance appraisals fail to accurately reflect employees' actual competencies and performance levels, they frequently result in dissatisfaction among both employees and managers, negatively influencing organizational efficiency and morale [12]. Park [13] highlighted that, to establish a more effective appraisal system, it was essential to consider the perspectives of employees and the motivational factors influencing managers/raters. 

Previous research has explored how rater motivation influences performance appraisal goals. Spence and Keeping [14] proposed four rating intentions: accuracy, conflict avoidance, benevolence, and impression management (i.e., controlling one's image). Khan et al. [15]. supported this framework by showing a significant relationship between rater motivation and appraisal effectiveness. Speer et al. [16] expanded this perspective by identifying five key motives: accuracy, coaching, encouragement, conflict avoidance, and system gaming, all of which shape rater behavior. Accuracy reflects the intent to rate employees in a way that objectively mirrors their performance.

Title: Validity And Reliability Rubric Of Performance Assessment Geometry Study In Junior High School Using The Many Facet Rasch Model Approach
